statement: The value, in dollars, of an investment $t$ years after it is made is modeled by $V(t) = 3{,}000e^{0.05t}$. To the nearest tenth of a year, how many years after the investment is made will its value be double its starting value?

choices.misconception: I treated the growth as yearly compounding at $5\%$ and solved $1.05^t = 2$, which gives about $14.2$, but the model uses $e^{0.05t}$.
I thought $5\%$ a year means it takes $\frac{100}{5} = 20$ years to gain $100\%$, ignoring that the growth compounds.
I got $e^{0.05t} = 2$ and then dropped the $e$, solving $0.05t = 2$ instead of taking the natural log of both sides.

hints: Divide both sides by $3{,}000$ to get $e^{0.05t} = 2$, then take the natural logarithm of both sides.

solutions.reliable: Set $3{,}000e^{0.05t} = 6{,}000$, so $e^{0.05t} = 2$. Taking natural logarithms, $0.05t = \ln 2 \approx 0.69315$, so $t \approx 13.863$, which rounds to $13.9$ years. Check: $3{,}000e^{0.05 \cdot 13.863} \approx 3{,}000 \cdot 2.000 = 6{,}000$.
solutions.elegant: The starting value $3{,}000$ does not matter: doubling needs $e^{0.05t} = 2$, so $t = \frac{\ln 2}{0.05} \approx 13.9$ for any starting amount.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
